name: Tomas Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a four-person distribution crew out of the Harlow depot, so mostly overhead lines on wooden poles across the farms and villages in the valley. Day starts at half six with the job sheets and a safety talk in the yard, then we're out in the bucket truck replacing rotten poles, swapping transformers, re-stringing a span a tractor clipped. I still write my switching steps on paper and read them back out loud to the control room, because that's how I was taught and nobody's ever been hurt on my crew. What I love is the end of a fault, when you close the switch and the farmhouse lights come back on across the field.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Storm call-outs, honestly. Last February I did nineteen hours straight after the ice took down the line along the Kessel road, and you're cold to the bone and still have to be sharp, because one mistake at eleven thousand volts and you don't go home. The other thing is the company sending new apps every six months to log our hours and photos. I'm the union steward for our depot, so I also spend my lunch break listening to people moan about rosters, which I don't mind, but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for two years: told you so. At the depot we'd have a laugh about the head office people who bought all the shiny software. Online I don't post much, but I'd probably share something about the money wasted on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on, which suits me fine. I'm twenty-seven, I've got the crew I want and I'm good at this. The only bit that would bother me is if the company still used AI as an excuse to squeeze rosters while not actually doing anything useful with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep putting a bit away each month, we've got about three months of bills saved and I want six. And I'd keep pushing at union meetings for clear rules on any new tech before it comes onto the trucks, because the hype comes back every few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company might use it as an excuse anyway. What would that look like on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's already started a little. Last spring they put in a scheduling program that said a pole change takes three hours, and it doesn't, not on a slope in the rain. My foreman two levels up said, the system says three, so I had to fight for every overtime hour. That's what I mean: the machine isn't clever, but they hide behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena talk about over dinner if this is how it goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, probably, and whether we finally rent the bigger flat near the hospital so her shifts are easier. She'd tease me for worrying about robots at all. With this one there'd be nothing to talk about, and I'd like that.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at the depot I'd called it, and laugh about the money head office wasted on shiny software. Online I'd maybe share something about the waste.
S0.think: Life carries on, and that suits me fine. My only worry is the company using AI as an excuse to squeeze rosters even when it doesn't do anything useful.
S0.do: Keeps saving towards six months of bills from the three he has now. Keeps pushing at union meetings for clear rules on any new technology before it reaches the trucks.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug about being right.
S0.quote: The machine isn't clever, but they hide behind it.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is proud, settled and suspicious of head office. His real issue isn't AI itself but management using any system as cover to cut hours, which he's already fought over a scheduling program. Calm here, with a steward's watchfulness underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, right, we need a proper agreement now, not later. I'd want the union to sit down with the company before any of it hits the depot. To friends I'd say it's going to be the office jobs first, the planners and the call centre, and we need to stand with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job mostly survives, but the shape of it changes and I won't like the new shape. They'll want me on a tablet all day, with some program telling me the order of jobs and checking my photos. And the younger ones coming in will learn on the screen first and the pole second, which scares me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get a technology clause onto the table at the next pay round, so no new system goes on the trucks without the crew trialling it. I'd keep saving, and I'd push for any retraining money to go to the planners and call centre staff who lose out. I'm not going to go learn AI myself unless I'm made to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my pay packet, more like something I care about is being taken out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the tools unless you're made to. What happens if your crew needs you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and Sanne, my apprentice, already uses one of those chat programs on her phone to look up regulations. If it came to it I'd let her show me, but I'd still check every switching step on paper. You don't trust a phone with your life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the company would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta in the control room, mostly. She's fifty-four, she's done fault dispatch for thirty years and knows every switch in the valley by heart. If a program starts routing the crews, they'll say she's not needed, and she's the one who's kept me safe on a dozen bad nights.

S1.say: At work I'd say we need a proper union agreement on the new tech now, before it hits the depot. To friends I'd say office jobs get hit first and we should stand with them.
S1.think: My job mostly survives, but it changes shape in ways I won't like, with tablets and programs checking my work. What scares me most is apprentices learning on the screen before the pole.
S1.do: Pushes for a technology clause at the next pay round so no system reaches the trucks without a crew trial. Keeps saving and argues for retraining money to go to planners and call centre staff.
S1.feel: Uneasy, less about pay than about losing control over work he cares about.
S1.quote: If a program starts routing the crews, they'll say she's not needed, and she's the one who's kept me safe on a dozen bad nights.
S1.fieldNote: His first instinct is collective: protect others before himself. He openly resists learning AI but softens when his apprentice is named. Worry centres on Marta in the control room, a strong sign his loyalty runs to people rather than the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the depot: this is the company's chance to sack everyone and they'll take it. I'd be at every union meeting and probably on the picket line if it came to that. Online I'd be the angry one, I can tell you that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot can climb a pole and work live lines by 2028, then I'm a skilled man with nothing to sell at twenty-seven. My diploma, my eight years on the tools, all of it worth nothing in two years. And I don't have a plan B, I never wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop any big spending, no bigger flat, no new car, and get our savings from three months up as fast as possible. I'd throw myself into the union, pushing for a law that a person has to be in charge of any work on the network, and for a fund for laid-off workers. I'd look at what jobs are left, maybe supervising the robots, but I'd be fighting for time first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It makes my chest tight just saying it. Two years isn't enough for anyone to do anything sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena the night you heard it was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd say, your job's safer than mine, and I hate that, because I always thought I'd be the steady one. She'd probably say, it's a hospital, they'll want robots there too. Then we'd sit there with the telly off not knowing what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a law needs a person in charge. Do you think a law could actually stop this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not stop it, no, I'm not daft. But slow it, and make the company pay for the people it drops. Two years is too fast for anyone to retrain, so somebody has to pull the brake, and it won't be the people making money from the robots.

S2.say: I'd say at the depot that this is the company's chance to sack everyone and they'll take it. I'd be at every union meeting, maybe on a picket line, and angry online.
S2.think: If a robot can work live lines by 2028, I'm a skilled man with nothing to sell at twenty-seven. I don't have a plan B and I never wanted one.
S2.do: Cancels big spending like the bigger flat and a new car, and builds savings fast beyond three months. Throws himself into union work for a law keeping a person in charge of network work and a fund for laid-off staff.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a tight chest and a sense that two years leaves no room for anything sensible.
S2.quote: Two years is too fast for anyone to retrain, so somebody has to pull the brake, and it won't be the people making money from the robots.
S2.fieldNote: This is where the resistance shows as fear: no plan B, and he says so plainly. His answer is to fight for time rather than adapt, through the union and the law. The moment with Lena, the telly off, was the most unguarded he got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but louder and earlier: get organised now while we've got time. I'd say it at the depot and I'd say it at the regional union meeting. Five years is long enough to win some rules if we start the day it's announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes me thirty-two, and that's still young enough to do something else, even if I'd hate it. The difference is I'd have a few years of good wages to save. But I'd spend those years watching it come up the road, which is its own kind of awful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd push savings towards six months and keep going on the union rules, same as the fast one. In year two or three I'd probably do a course, maybe electrical inspection or something on the safety side, where a person still has to sign things off. I'd wait a bit to see what actually stays human before picking, though, because I'm not throwing my trade away early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's pressure I can push against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see before picking a course. How long would you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two years, I think. If by then the company's running robot trials on the trucks, I'd go. If they're still struggling to get a drone to read a pole tag, I'd stay put a bit longer. I'm slow, but I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Sanne, your apprentice, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to finish her ticket, because a ticket's worth having whatever happens, then go and study something on the side. She's quicker with the technology than me. She'd have more chance in five years than I would, and I'd want her to use it.

S3.say: I'd say get organised now while there's time, at the depot and at the regional union meeting. Five years is long enough to win some rules if we start straight away.
S3.think: Five years makes me thirty-two, still young enough to do something else, even if I'd hate it. I'd have a few years of wages to save, but I'd spend them watching it come up the road.
S3.do: Builds savings towards six months in year one while pushing union rules. Waits about two years to see what stays human, then plans a course in inspection or safety work where a person signs things off.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to push against it, not frozen.
S3.quote: If they're still struggling to get a drone to read a pole tag, I'd stay put a bit longer. I'm slow, but I'm not stupid.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he moves from pure resistance to a reluctant plan, but still waits for proof before committing. He sees his apprentice as better placed than himself, which he admits without bitterness. Says and thinks line up closely for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do it properly, so no excuses. At work I'd be pushing for a long-term deal: retraining paid for by the company, early warning on cuts. Online I'd probably share stuff about the old miners and how badly they were treated, as a warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the cruel one for someone my age. It means I give the best years of my working life to a trade that's ending, and at thirty-seven I start again. An older lineworker could ride it out to retirement. I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd keep working, keep the union pushing, and keep saving like before. Around year three I'd start an evening course, probably as an electrical inspector or a safety assessor, because the company will still need someone to answer for things when it goes wrong. I'd want it paid for by the company and I'd fight for that before I paid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a slow, grinding way rather than a sharp one. Like a bad knee you know is going to get worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said ten years is enough for a government to act, and also that it's the cruel one for you. How do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I hear it. Both are true, I think. It's enough time for the country to cope, but it doesn't make it any less of a loss for me personally, it just stretches it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture yourself at thirty-seven when it arrives. Where are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully in an inspector's van with a clipboard, still out on the network, still in the valley. Maybe Lena and I have kids by then, I don't know. What I don't want is to be in a training room at thirty-seven with a lot of other men my age, being told it'll be fine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for governments to do it properly, so no excuses, and push for company-paid retraining and early warning on cuts. Online I'd share stories about how badly old miners were treated.
S4.think: Ten years is the cruel one for someone my age. I give my best working years to a trade that's ending and start again at thirty-seven, while older lineworkers can ride it out.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving in year one while the union pushes for a long-term deal. From around year three takes an evening course as an electrical inspector or safety assessor, fighting first for the company to pay.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow, grinding way, like a bad knee he knows will get worse.
S4.quote: It means I give the best years of my working life to a trade that's ending, and at thirty-seven I start again.
S4.fieldNote: A strong age effect: he sees a decade as worse for him than for older colleagues, not better. He accepts the gentle challenge on his two views without getting defensive. His picture of the future is still on the network, in the valley, with a clipboard rather than a hook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years and the trade I've built my life on is gone, and I'm too young to retire and too set in my ways to jump fast. What would help is a law that says a qualified person has to be in charge of work on the grid, and real money for retraining that's paid by the companies making the savings, not by me out of my three months' savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if they rush robots onto live lines, somebody's going to get hurt, maybe a farmer, maybe a kid near a downed wire. I'd want the people who know the network in the room when they decide how it's done.

headlineQuote: What I love is the end of a fault, when you close the switch and the farmhouse lights come back on across the field.
portrait: Tomas Weber is a 27-year-old crew leader on overhead distribution lines out of the Harlow depot, and the union steward there. He lives with his partner Lena, a hospital nurse, and has about three months of bills saved. He trusts paper, people and his own hands, and distrusts head office and its software. He's calm if AI stalls, uneasy and union-minded under steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because he has no plan B. With more warning he reluctantly plans a move into inspection or safety work, but sees ten years as cruel for someone his age.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his trade would be gone in two years while he's too young to retire and too set in his ways to jump fast.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a qualified person to be in charge of work on the grid, and retraining paid for by the companies making the savings.
